en: *Abhisamayamañjarī* by Śubhākaragupta,
edited by the Rare Buddhist Texts Series, No. 11 (Sarnath, 1993).
The emendation proposed by the editor is indicated within brackets: *eṅ*. *viśuddhiskandhādisamutthaḥ* (emended to *-samutthaṃ*).
The emendations proposed by others are shown as follows:
Eṅ. *Abhisamayamañjarī*, beginning with the section on the Pure Aggregates and so forth. (Emended by Tanemura from *-samutthaḥ* to *-samuttaṃ*; text begins)
Oṃ, homage to Vajravārāhī;
homage be to Vajrayoginī, whose essence is emptiness and compassion,
who assumes a manifold variety of forms according to the diverse natures of worldly existence.
That which is indeed illuminated by clarity through the power of the nectar-grove of the nectar of perfect enlightenment;
[that which is illuminated by clarity].
The peaceful [deity] and the others spread redness outside due to the passion of the people to be trained;
though peaceful,
she bears a vajra, a stainless skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga, possessing fierce radiance.
May this Blessed Lady, Ugrajyotis Vajravilāsinī, be for your prosperity.

In this practice, the yogi—possessing undivided faith in the Guru and the Buddha, having properly grasped the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), and having correctly received initiation—faces south (*dakṣiṇābhimukha*), with his mass of hair loosened and his mouth purified by the application of the five powders (*pañcavaṭikā*) and so forth; he sits upon a comfortable seat in a certain place such as a cemetery or a mountain, or else sits directly upon a corpse in a cemetery.

Having recited three times the sequence of vowels and consonants— *oṃ a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha ja jha ña ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ta tha da dha na pa pha ba bha ma ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha kṣa huṃ huṃ phaṭ*— which is throbbing with five-colored rays and stands encircling [the practitioner], one should visualize the host of deities of the three wheels, who have crushed the hosts of obstructors.
This is the purification of speech (*vāgviśuddhi*).
One should resolve upon the purity of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, because acts such as worship arising from the purified aggregates and so forth become a swift cause for enlightenment.

In that regard, Vairocana and the other [deities] are to be determined as being like foam, bubbles, a mirage, a plantain tree, and an illusion, within the range of form up to consciousness. Akṣobhya is [to be resolved] in *tathatā* (suchness).
Alternatively, their very purity is the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) upon the deities Vairocana and the others.
One should summon the heroic yoginīs residing in the world-systems of the ten directions.
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga.
Oṃ āḥ aralli hoḥ jaḥ hūṃ ho vajraḍākinī, you are the commitment! Hoḥ!
One should offer the bali with the vajra-añjali mudrā, the gesture of the upward-flowering [lotus].

Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi! May all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, apasmāras, ḍākas, ḍākinīs, and so forth, accept this bali offering; may they protect the samaya; for the purpose of eating, drinking, and smelling, do not transgress; be my helpers for the sake of increasing all happiness through [the attainment of] my omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! This is the purification of the bali mantra. [The purification of the bali mantra for those residing in the world-systems of the ten directions. Oṃ.
In that regard, within form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there are Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Vajrasattva.
Within the suchness of form and the other aggregates, there is Akṣobhya.
These six are to be understood by their colors as white, yellow, red, green, white, and black.
According to the *Coll.* up to this point:

Vairocana has his right hand raised holding a wheel, and his left hand at his hip holding a bell together with a lotus. Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi have their right arms gracefully raised holding, respectively, a jewel, a red lotus, and a crossed-vajra; their left hands hold bells at their hips.

Vajrasattva holds a vajra in his right hand placed gracefully at his heart, and his left hand holding a bell rests proudly at his hip. Akṣobhyavajra holds a vajra in his right hand joined with the earth-touching mudrā, and his left hand holding a bell rests proudly at his hip.

In the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and tactile sense, there are Mohavajra, Dveṣavajra, Īrṣyāvajra, Rāgavajra, and Mātsaryavajra; their internal names are Kṣitigarbha, Vajrapāṇi, Khagarbha, Lokeśvara, and Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin; they are white, black, yellow, red, and dark green in color.

In all the sense bases (āyatana), there is Aiśvaryavajra, whose internal name is Samantabhadra, and he is white. Mohavajra has his right hand raised in a threatening gesture (cakrodyata) and his left hand gracefully holding a bell at his heart.
Dveṣavajra has his right hand at his heart holding a vajra, and his left hand, adorned with a bell, resting proudly at his hip.

Īrṣyāvajra, Rāgavajra, and Mātsaryavajra have their right arms gracefully raised, holding respectively a jewel, a red lotus, and a double-vajra; their left hands, adorned with bells, rest gracefully at their hearts. Aiśvaryavajra, however, has his right hand at his heart holding a vajra, and his left hand, adorned with a bell, resting at his hip.

In this context, he is Mohavajra because of the destruction of delusion; Dveṣavajra because of the hatred of hatred; and the three beginning with Īrṣyāvajra because of the destruction of envy, all attachment, and stinginess.
He is Aiśvaryavajra because of the bestowing of all sovereignty;
these have as their essential nature the purification of the elements of earth, water, fire, and air.
Pātanī, Māraṇī, Ākarṣaṇī, and Narteśvarī are yellow, black, red, and green in color respectively; they each have one face and four arms.
Their two right hands hold a discus-sword, a vajra-sword, a lotus-sword, and a scimitar-sword, while their two left hands hold a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff.
Rocanā (also known as Locanā), Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā have the nature of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).

Padmajālinī is smoke-colored, with three faces—smoke, white, and red—and six arms; her three left arms hold a skull-cup (*kapāla*), a khaṭvāṅga, and a noose, while her three right arms are adorned with a hook (*aṅkuśa*), a Brahma-head, and a flaying knife (*kartī*); she has the nature of the Vajra of the Dharma-element (*dharmadhātuvajra*).
In this context, Pātanyā and the others accomplish activities according to their respective names.
Vairocana and the others stand in the *ālīḍha* posture, wear crowns of matted hair, possess three eyes, and are adorned with the five mudrās.
The two [consorts] have loose hair, are naked, stand in the *ālīḍha* posture, possess three eyes, and bear the five mudrās.

Then, having visualized within the hollow of one's own heart a red syllable *vaṃ* situated upon a solar disc produced from the seed-syllable *raṃ*, and having dispelled internal impurities by its rays, one should draw forth, through rays emerging from every pore of the skin, the previously mentioned maṇḍala-circle of the Bhagavatī, as well as the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas; having brought them into the sky before oneself, one should pay homage and worship them with the sixteen goddesses beginning with Vīṇā, who have been projected by the rays of the seed-syllable.

Therein, the Vīṇā, Vaṃśā, Mṛdaṅgā, and Murajā goddesses have one face and four arms; they are blue, yellow, red, and green respectively, and are intent upon playing their respective instruments, holding a *vajra* and a *vajraghaṇṭā* in their two principal hands.
Hāsyā, Lāsyā, Gītā, and Nṛtyā have one face and four arms; they are reddish-brown, blue, yellow, and green respectively.
Hāsyā and Lāsyā perform the gestures of laughter and dance with their two principal hands.
Lāsyā has two principal arms performing the proud (or womb-like) *lāsya* gesture while holding a vajra and a vajra-bell;
Gītā has two principal arms holding a *kaṃsīkā* [cymbal].
Nṛtyā has two arms primarily engaged in the gestures of the lotus;
the other right and left arms of these [deities] hold a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff.
Puṣpā, Dhūpā, Dīpā, and Gandhā are white, smoke-colored, flame-colored, and red in hue respectively; they have four arms and one face.

Among these, [the goddesses] Āśā hold a flower-vase, an incense burner, a lamp-stick, and a perfume conch in their primary right hands; in their other three left hands, they hold a *ḍamaru* drum, a skull-cup, and a *khaṭvāṅga*.

Ādarśā, Rasā, Sparśā, and Dharmā are white, red, green, and white respectively; they have four arms and one face, and in their primary right hand they hold a mirror, a vessel of nectar, a *viśvavajra*, and the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), while in their other three left hands they hold a *ḍamaru* drum, a skull-cup, and a *khaṭvāṅga*.

Thereafter, having praised [the Buddha] with the eight-line mantras to be recited next, and having performed the sevenfold unsurpassed worship—consisting of the confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, the aspiration for nirvāṇa, the request for the long endurance of the Victors, the entreaty for the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the supplication to the Buddhas, and the dedication of one’s own merit—one should, preceded by taking refuge in the Three Jewels, relying upon the path of the Victors, offering up one’s own person, and generating the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), regard all sentient beings as if they were one’s only son.

In the same way, having cultivated: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which consists of the desire for union with the single flavor of great bliss; compassion (*karuṇā*), which takes the form of the wish to remove suffering; sympathetic joy (*muditā*), which has the nature of the desire not to be separated from the enjoyments, sovereignty, and so forth arising from roots of virtue; and equanimity (*upekṣā*), which is characterized by proceeding spontaneously within the reality (*dharmatā*) that is free from both aversion and attachment in all things; and having thus accumulated the equipment of merit, one should recite for the sake of increasing the equipment of wisdom: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho ’ham*.
Thus, one should recite this preceded by bringing the meaning to mind.
Here, "all phenomena are pure by nature" is the purification of the object (*grāhya-viśuddhi*); "I am pure by nature" is the purification of the subject (*grāhaka-viśuddhi*).
Just as a magician, having conjured an illusion, withdraws it again—
Nothing whatsoever exists there; for that is the true nature of phenomena.
Thus, according to the scriptural teaching:

having caused the three realms and the invited maṇḍala-circle—which are of the nature of mere appearance—to enter into the clear light itself, and having dissolved oneself into the sun, that [sun] into the syllable *vaṃ*, that into the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), that into the bindu, and that into the *nāda*, one should even dissolve that conceptualization [into the ultimate], thinking:
"I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness (*oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*)."
Having recited this while recollecting its meaning, one should relinquish [the breath].
"Vajra" is the very gnosis of emptiness because of its indivisibility; the meaning is: "I am of the nature of that, having its essence."

Then, by the force of the momentum of previous consecration, having emerged from the meditative absorption on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), one should contemplate one's own mind as transforming, one above the other, into the syllables *yaṃ*, *raṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *laṃ*. These take the form of a bow, a triangle, a circle, and a square, colored blue, red, white, and yellow respectively; they are marked with two tips like fluttering banners, adorned with flames and bells, and possess the four corners that have the nature of the mandalas of wind, fire, water, and earth. Above that, one should contemplate a square mountain with eight peaks, arisen from the syllable *suṃ*.
Having visualized Mount Sumeru as consisting of silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and gold on its eastern, southern, western, and northern sides, one then recites:
*oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha huṃ hūṃ phaṭ* / *oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa huṃ hūṃ phaṭ* /

"Oṃ gṛhṇāya 2 huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ ānaya ho bhagavan vidyārāja huṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Having recited these four mantras while snapping the thumb and forefinger of the left hand to cast them forth, one should visualize four vajra-walls of black, green, red, and yellow color, possessing massive bodies that blaze, pervading the entire universe from the peak of Brahmā’s egg down to the subterranean realm (rasātala), extending as far as desired in the east, north, west, and south respectively by means of the light rays of the *Sumbha* and other mantras.
Having uttered "Oṃ vajraprākāra hūṃ vaṃ hūṃ," one should establish [the enclosure].
At that very same moment, with a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) produced from and empowered by the syllable *huṃ*, [one recites]:
"Oṃ medinī vajrībhava vajrabandha hūṃ."
Having recited this, one should preside over the ground consisting of the universal vajra, extending down to the limits of the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Then, with the vajra-rays:
*oṃ vajraśarajvala traṃ saṃ traṃ*.
Having spoken thus, [he visualizes] a very dense net of arrows above in the form of a five-pronged vajra; below that, having uttered "HŪṂ VAṂ HŪṂ," the vajra-fence;
and having uttered "OṂ VAJRAVITĀNA HŪṂ KHAṂ HŪṂ," the vajra-canopy in its proper place.
Having uttered "Oṃ vajrajvālānalārka hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ," one should visualize the vajra-flame.

Thereafter, one should visualize the four goddesses, Kākāsyā and the others, who are produced from the four mantras beginning with *sumbha*, as well as the four goddesses, Yamadāḍhī and the others, who are born from the rays of light of those same two sets of mantras.

These [deities] have two arms and one face; from below the navel they have the form of a trident. Holding a vajra-mallet in the right hand and a kīla in the form of their own body in the left, they go forth by means of emanation and, having summoned the hosts of obstructors situated in the ten directions, they cause them to enter the wells located in the cardinal and intermediate directions outside the vajra-fence produced by the long-sounding utterance of the syllable *huṃ*. *Oṃ gha gha ghāṭaya ghāṭaya sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ phaṭ kīlaya kīlaya sarvapāpān phaṭ phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ.*

"O Vajra, nail down! O Vajradhara, by his command, nail down all obstacles; nail down the vajras of body, speech, and mind! HŪṂ PHAṬ!"—thus they strike, preceded by the recitation of this striking mantra.
One should meditate on her making the multitude of obstacles one with great bliss through striking and piercing.

Then, having driven away the remaining obstacles, as they dissolve into the ramparts, one should contemplate circular ramparts of vajras, lotuses, and wheels for the purpose of binding the boundary, according to the principle of the emergence of water-drops from the pervasion of water.

Thus, having resolved that the world is free from obstacles and has become a single, seamless expanse through the purification of the expulsion of impediments such as the vajra-fence, one should contemplate within the vajra-pavilion a *dharmodayā*—the nature of the *dharmadhātu*—in the form of the syllable *E*, which is wide at the top and narrow at the bottom. In its center, upon a universal lotus and universal vajra, stands a peaked palace (*kūṭāgāra*) consisting of Vidyāvairocana born from the seed-syllable *Huṃ*; for there is no disparity between a Tathāgata and an ordinary person, since both are of the same singular nature in *tathatā*.

It has four corners through the foundations of mindfulness; it has four gates through the purity of the right exertions and the bases of psychic power; it is adorned with eight pillars through the purity of the eightfold path; and it is purified by the four concentrations: Śūraṅgama, Gaganagañja, Vimalamudrā, and Siṃhavikrīḍita.

It is surrounded by four goddesses; it is adorned with four archways through the purity of the four dhyānas; it is embellished with necklaces, half-necklaces, moons, suns, banners, mirrors, and chowries through the purity of the seven factors of enlightenment; in brief, however, it is endowed with those characteristics through the purity of the various qualities of a Buddha.

In his navel, one should visualize the eight worldly dharmas as being purified within the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus born from a red syllable *paṃ*. Through the purification that dispels the darkness of ignorance, there is a solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*) produced from the doubling of the vowels (*ali*). Within this is a lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*) whose nature is the mirror-like wisdom (*darśajñāna*), produced from the doubling of the consonants (*kāli*). The union of these two discs—the solar disc whose nature is the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) and the lunar disc—is the Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*) of their meeting. In the center of this union is a red syllable *vaṃ*, from which arises a vajra-fist; within it resides the seed-syllable *vaṃ* upon a sun-disk.

The knowledge of performance (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) consists of pervading with rays emanated from that [wisdom] which has the nature of the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), performing the welfare of sentient beings in the form of the Bhagavatī throughout the ten directions, and then withdrawing them back into that very same place.

Through the transformation of all this, one visualizes oneself as the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī, whose intrinsic nature is the wisdom of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*. By virtue of the purification of great passion (*mahārāga*), she resembles the color of a pomegranate flower; by virtue of the purification of the two truths, she has two arms. With her right hand, the index finger extended upward, she is intent on threatening the wicked; by virtue of the purification of the five wisdoms merged into a single flavor, she holds a red vajra. In her left hand, held downward, she holds a dry and fresh corpse impaled upon a staff topped with a single-pronged and upward-pointing black five-pronged vajra.

Her staff-like arms, whose nature is skillful means, are adorned with a universal banner featuring a fine bell that rings from the base of a golden vase marked with a double-vajra; she holds a white *kaṭvāṅga* and a skull-cup filled with blood—the essence of great bliss and great compassion—attached [to her arms]. She has one distorted face as a sign of the abandonment of false views, is terrifying with prominent fangs due to the destruction of the four Māras, and has eyes red with compassion purified in body, speech, and mind.

For the sake of purifying the scattering of the reality of non-duality (*advaitatattva*) through the eighty-four thousand heaps of Dharma, she has loose hair and wears the five mudrās known as the discus (*cakrin*), the earring (*kuṇḍala*), the necklace (*kaṇṭhikā*), the breast-ornament (*rucaka*), and the girdle (*mekhalā*).
She is adorned with a necklace, a breast-ornament, earrings, and a crest-jewel.
The sacred thread and the ashes—these are proclaimed as the six mudrās.
Thus say some.
Others say she is marked with the six seals as the mistress of the mandala.

She is naked, endowed with the bloom of youth, and her nature is the fifty letters of the alphabet (*ālikāli*). She wears a garland of freshly severed human heads strung together. With her left leg drawn in—indicating emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signaling the world through the *ālīḍha* stance—and her right leg extended five spans, she stands in *ālīḍha* posture upon a sun disc atop a red eight-petaled lotus, treading upon Bhairava and Kālarātri, whose natures are the conceptualizations of eternalism and nihilism. This is due to her union with the light of perfectly pure primordial wisdom (*suviśuddhajñāna*).

She possesses a halo of solar radiance; because she is the form of emptiness, she is of great brilliance due to her equality with the non-apprehension of the world. From the union of passion (*raja-yoga*), she flows [with nectar]; she is fond of blood due to her constant engagement in drinking the blood flowing from the skull-cup held in her hand. She has three topknots bound by a garland of skulls consisting of the five Tathāgatas situated between two rows of vajras. Because she bestows grace upon all, her crown is pressed down by a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*); because she encompasses all world-systems...

One should meditate on the eight consciousnesses—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and the afflicted mental consciousness (*kliṣṭamanovijñāna*)—as being situated within the eight charnel grounds because they lack the nature of a self.

As for the fact that in the *Abhisamaya* of Lūyīpāda the meditation on emptiness is taught immediately after the protection of the vajra-cage and so forth, that is due to the context of those with superior wisdom;
for such a person, emptiness itself is the supreme protection.

Furthermore, regarding the gathering of all beings, after the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the "protective cage" (*rakṣāpañjara*) and so forth are taught here; moreover, this very sequence is observed in many *abhisamayas*.
On the four petals in the east and other directions, turning counter-clockwise, there are in order Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī.
They are black, green, red, and fair-complexioned respectively; they have one face and four arms, holding a *khaṭvāṅga* and a skull-cup in their left hands.

To the right, they should be meditated upon as holding a *ḍamaru* drum and a flaying knife, three-eyed, with faces terrifying with bared fangs, with loose hair, naked, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, wearing the five mudrās, adorned with garlands of severed heads, having a vajra-garland on their foreheads and a girdle, and decorated with tinkling bells and other ornaments.

In the lotus vessels located in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast, turning clockwise, one should meditate upon four lotus bowls filled with the essence of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), with menstrual blood (*rajas*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and the five lamps— all of which have become like nectar through the power of the elixir of accomplishment (*siddharasa*).

Outside of that, encircled by a garland of blue vajras, is the first mind-wheel (*citta-cakra*) with eight spokes. On its eastern, northern, western, and southern spokes—which possess the nature of the *pīṭhas* of Pullīramalaya, Jālandhara, Oḍiyāna, and Arbuda—reside Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍākṣī, Prabhāvatī, and Mahānāsā.
On the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast spokes—which consist of the *upapīṭhas* of Godāvarī, Rāmeśvara, Devīkoṭṭa, and Mālava—reside Vīramatī, Kharvarī, Laṅkeśvarī, and Drumacchāyā.

In the second speech-wheel (*vākcakra*), which is red and surrounded by a row of red lotuses, there are eight spokes. On the eastern and northern spokes, corresponding to the sacred fields (*kṣetra*) of Kāmarūpa and Oḍra, are Airāvatī and Mahābhairavā. On the western and southern spokes, corresponding to the secondary fields (*upakṣetra*) of Triśakuni and Kośala, are Vāyuvegā and Surābhakṣī.
In the southeast and southwest, corresponding to the *chandoha* sites of Kaliṅga and Lampāka, are Śyāmadevī and Subhadrā.
In the northwest and northeast, corresponding to the *upacchandoha* sites of Kāñcī and Himālaya, are Hayakarṇā and Khagānanā.

In the third body-wheel (*kāyacakra*), which is white and surrounded by a circle of white spokes, Cakravegā and Khaṇḍarohā reside on the eastern and northern spokes at the meeting points (*melāpaka*) of Pretapurī and Gṛhadevatā;
Śauṇḍinī and Cakravarmiṇī reside on the western and southern spokes at the meeting points of Saurāṣṭra and Suvarṇadvīpa;

and Cakravartinī and Mahāvīryā reside on the southeastern and southwestern spokes at the cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*) of Nagara and Sindhu, and the secondary cremation grounds (*upaśmaśāna*) of Maru and Kulūta.
These goddesses, Pracaṇḍā and the others, have one face and two arms; they hold a skull-cup filled with blood in their left hand and a threatening knife in their right.
Furthermore, their dress, ornaments, and so forth are like those of the Ḍākinīs and others.
At the gates are Kākāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, Śvānāsyā, and Śūkarāsyā, who are like the Ḍākinīs and others.
The faces of these supreme goddesses correspond to their names.

In the corners are Yamadāḍhī, Yamadūtī, Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī, and Yamamathani; they have human faces, and the bodies of the deities of the right and left directions are half-bodies resembling the right and left halves of the [central] body.
These eight are also the Śvāsanās.
The remaining attire and so forth are exactly like those of the ḍākinīs and others.
All these goddesses are to be seen as being instantaneously perfected at the very same moment that the Bhagavatī is perfected.
Then, having performed the visualization of the Wheel of Knowledge (*jñānacakra*), one should perform the protective armor (*rakṣākavaca*) as taught by Lūyīpāda with the words:

"Having purified the sense-bases (*āyatana*) with the syllables *bhrūṃ hūṃ khaṃ aḥ hāṃ ha*, one should arm oneself with the armor of Nairātmya, just like one's own respective deity, using the mantras of the six goddesses—Vārāhī, Yāminī, Mohinī, Sañcāriṇī, Saṃtrāsinī, and Caṇḍikā.
*Oṃ vaṃ* at the navel.
Hāṃ yāṃ in the heart; hrīṃ moṃ in the face;
heṃ hīṃ on the head.
HŪṂ HŪṂ at the crest-lock;
PHAṬ PHAṬ on all limbs as the weapon-mantra.
Alternatively, because there is no difference between the mantra and the deity, those very deities—having been generated in the respective minds—should be meditated upon in those various locations.
Therein, Vārāhī has faces that are red, blue, and green; she holds a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga, and a noose in her left hands, and a goad, a Brahma-head, and a flaying-knife in her right hands.

Yāminī, Mohinī, Sañcāriṇī, Saṃtrāsinī, and Caṇḍikā are blue, white, yellow, green, and smoke-colored respectively; they have four arms and hold a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga, and a bell in their left hands, while holding a hand-drum and a flaying-knife in their right hands. All of them should be visualized with loose hair, naked, three-eyed, and standing in the ālīḍha posture.

Thereafter, one should place the syllables Oṃ, Āḥ, and Hūṃ—white, red, and blue respectively—upon the forehead, throat, and heart. Then, from the seed-syllable Vaṃ situated upon the sun-maṇḍala atop a red eight-petaled lotus at the center of the heart, within the hub of a red vajra, rays of light emanate. These rays attract the Wisdom Circle (jñānacakra), which has manifested as the form of all the heroes and heroines residing in the ten directions. Having invoked them with the syllable Jaḥ and worshipped them with offerings such as water for the feet preceded by the lute-playing goddesses and others, one should recite the syllable Phem, bind the Jāla-mudrā, and rotate it on the forehead in a counter-clockwise direction.

Having caused [the wisdom-circle] to enter one's own commitment-circle like water into water by means of the syllable *HŪṂ*, having bound it with the syllable *VAṂ*, and having gratified it with the syllable *HOḤ*, one should recite: "Oṃ! All phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga.

Simultaneously with the summoning of the wisdom-circle, [the practitioner is honored] by the Vajravilāsinīs who have been summoned, who hold skull-cups and hand-drums filled with the nectar of wisdom, and who are worshipped by deities such as Vīṇā who have emerged from the seed-syllable at the heart.
Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon birth,
so shall I bathe you with pure, divine water.

Thus, having visualized oneself as the essence of great bliss being consecrated by streams of the nectar of gnosis emerging from the skull-cups held in the slightly bent left hands of those reciting [the mantra], and having contemplated the Tathāgatas produced from the remaining water upon one's head, one should empower [the self] with: *oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekataḥ samayaśriye hūṃ*.

In that regard, Vairocana is the Lord of the Family for the Bhagavatī on her head; Ratnasambhava is for the Ḍākinīs and the others; Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Śāśvata are respectively for those situated in the mind, speech, and body wheels; and Amoghasiddhi is for those residing in the commitment wheel.
Afterwards, one should perform the tasting of nectar.

By means of the syllable *yaṃ*, there arises a wind mandala; above that, a fire mandala born from the syllable *raṃ*; therein, a white lotus vessel born from the white syllable *āḥ*, topped with a crest made of three severed heads. Having produced the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*) presided over by the syllables *oṃ traṃ aṃ khaṃ hūṃ lāṃ māṃ pāṃ tāṃ* situated therein, one observes them as having the form of a molten liquid, the color of the newly risen sun, as the seed-syllables and so forth have melted through the heat of the fire ignited and fanned by the wind. Then, having moved upward from that [liquid] a distance of one span (*vitasti*),...

Having visualized a white *khaṭvāṅga* made of nectar, with a white *HŪṂ* facing downward, one should contemplate that [liquid] as cool, flowing like mercury, having dissolved therein through the touch of its vapor upon falling. Then, having visualized the three syllables one above the other on top of that, one should draw in the nectar of primordial wisdom residing in the hearts of all the Tathāgatas, together with all the nectar existing within the belly of the three worlds, by means of their rays; having absorbed it into that very place, and once the three syllables have also gradually dissolved, then again—

Having empowered oneself with the three-syllable mantra, one should meditate on a white vajra the size of a *jaya* fruit, marked with a white *hūṃ*, upon the tongues of the deities of the mandala; then, by means of the tubes of its rays, one should perform the consumption [of the nectar].
Thereafter, one should praise with the eight-line worship mantras to be described below.

If one is unable to stabilize the mind for a long time within this vast wheel of the mandala, then [one should focus] on the line of light-rays arising from the lotus-fiber of the seed-syllable *vaṃ* situated within the union of the sun and moon at the navel-lotus.

By means of stabilizing the mind, through the avoidance of the flow in the two channels of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, there is entry into the central channel (*madhyamā*). When [the winds] have blazed and been melted by the *caṇḍālī*, through the sequence of pervading the lunar wheel (*śaśicakra*) at the head, the innate (*sahaja*) arises via the distinctions of bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth. Therein, due to the withdrawal of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), there is either the simultaneous non-perception of the mandala-circle or its gradual absorption into emptiness (*śūnyatā*). In this regard, the sequence is as follows:

The world is in the cremation grounds; the cremation grounds are in the outer wheel (*bāhyacakra*); the outer wheel is in the body wheel (*kāyacakra*); the body wheel is in the speech wheel (*vākcakra*); the speech wheel is in the mind wheel (*cittacakra*). Within the mind wheel, those situated in the cardinal directions are among the *ḍākinīs* and so forth, while those situated in the intermediate directions are among the *rūpiṇīs* and so forth. The *ḍākinīs* and others are situated in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) within the mouth of the Blessed Lady. The lotus seat of the Blessed Lady is upon the sun; the sun is upon Bhairava; Bhairava is upon Kālarātri; Kālarātri is upon the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*); the skull-topped staff is upon the Blessed Lady; and the Blessed Lady...

Within the navel-lotus, one should dissolve the navel-lotus into the union of sun and moon; the union of sun and moon into the syllable *vaṃ*; the syllable *vaṃ* into the half-moon; the half-moon into the drop (*bindu*); and the drop into the resonance (*nāda*). One should then perceive even that resonance as having the form of a hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair.
Yet, in the highest degree, even that is not perceived.
In this way, by virtue of being the nature of the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*), there is the entry of the Blessed Lady into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*).
In this manner, one should repeatedly enter and emerge.
As it has been said:
"Just as the breath-wind dissolves from all sides into a mirror,"
In that same way, the yogin should enter the limit of reality again and again.
Through repeated entries, the yogin directly realizes the yuganaddha-samādhi, which is perfected as the non-differentiation of the two truths.

When weariness arises, he should place his mind upon the syllable *vaṃ* situated at the navel-lotus; then, at the very moment of reciting either the *hṛdaya* or *upahṛdaya* mantra as desired from among those to be mentioned below, he should, together with the wind exiting through the sound of that seed-syllable, cause the five wheels to revolve and perform the welfare of the world. At the time of the [wind's] re-entry, he should cause it to enter back into that very same [seed-syllable] along with the mantra, according to the principle of pulling in a thread from a rosary.

However, for those who desire to perform the recitation of the mantras of the individual goddesses that are about to be described, at the conclusion of the utterance of each individual goddess's mantra, the emanation and reabsorption of each must be performed as previously stated.

Alternatively, one should visualize the garland of syllables rising from that very place as before, emerging from the mouth via the path of the *avadhūtī*, returning to its own place in the lotus, and revolving there in the same manner; or one should recite either the *hṛdaya* or *upahṛdaya* mantra, or the *mālāmantra* to be described later.

Or else, while gazing at that very seed-syllable as a garland of mantras like a circle of lamps, one should perform the recitation—neither too fast nor too slow, and free from improper mental constructs—as follows:
*oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The heart mantra of the Bhagavatī is:
Oṃ vajravairocanīye svāhā. This also is a heart mantra.
Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
This is the subsidiary heart mantra (upahṛdaya-mantra).
These mantras possess great power.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Vajravārāhī! Vaṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, homage to the Noble Aparājitā, Mother of the Three Worlds, Sovereign of Great Knowledge! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, homage to the one who brings fear to all spirits, the Great Vajra! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, homage to the one seated on the vajra, the unconquered, the unconquerable, the subduer, the one who causes the eyes to whirl, *huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*!
Oṃ, homage to the witherer, the inflamer, the wrathful and formidable one, *huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*! Oṃ, homage to the terrifier, the slayer, the divider, the unconquered one, *huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*!
Oṃ, homage to Jayā, Vijayā, Jambhanī, Stambhanī, Mohanī, huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, homage to Vajravārāhī, Mahāyogeśvarī, Khage, huṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
This is the eight-line mantra for worship of the Blessed Lady.

And furthermore, the garland mantra (*mālāmantra*) is as follows: Oṃ Vajravārāhī! O you who pierce the vital points, pierce them! Strike, strike the life-breaths! Kiṃkini khiṃkhini! Shake, shake! O you who hold a vajra in your hand! Dry up, dry up! O you who bear the vajra-khaṭvāṅga and skull-cup! O you who devour great flesh and meat! O you who are clothed in human entrails! O you who wear a garland of human heads knotted together! Sumbha nisumbha! Strike, strike the life-breaths! Destroy all the sins of sentient beings and all animals! O cutter of great flesh! O embodiment of wrath! O you with terrifying fangs! O Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*)!

O foremost queen of the god Śrī Heruka! You who possess a thousand heads, a thousand arms, and a hundred thousand faces; you of blazing splendor, with a flaming mouth, tawny eyes, and a vajra-body; you seated upon the vajra-throne! Mili mili! Timili timili! He he! Ha ha! Huṃ hūṃ! Kha kha! Dhu dhu! Ru ru! Dhuru dhuru! Muru muru! O non-dual Great Yoginī, perfected by recitation! Drauṃ dhaṃ draṃ dhaṃ graṃ! He he! O terrible one! Hasa hasa! O heroine! Hā hā! Ho ho! Huṃ hūṃ! O destroyer of the three worlds!

*Śatasahasrakoṭitathāgataparivāre huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! O you in the form of a lion, *khaḥ*; in the form of an elephant, *gaḥ*; O you whose belly is the three worlds, whose girdle is the great ocean, swallow, swallow, *huṃ hūṃ phaṭ!* O non-dual hero, *huṃ hūṃ hā hā!* O you who delude the great noose, O Mistress of Yoga (*yogeśvarī*), you are the ḍākinī of the worlds, worthy of homage, and one who produces immediate conviction, *huṃ hūṃ phaṭ!* O terrifier of spirits, O Great Hero, O Supreme Siddha, O Mistress of Yoga, *phaṭ huṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!* (13–14) This mantra of great power is accomplished through recitation alone.
During a lunar eclipse, one should recite [the mantra] while gazing at the moon until the moon is released;
thereafter, as long as one continues to repeat it, one will be followed by thousands of women.

Following the practice of meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*), by merely uttering the words, one attracts, kills, and performs the rites of eradication, inciting enmity, and paralyzing those with cruel minds.
If one casts charcoal from a cremation ground into a house, a village, or a city after reciting the mantra once over it, it causes a conflagration;
if one waves a peacock feather in the air, it subsides again.
Such are its many kinds of powers described elsewhere.
Oṃ ḍākinīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ, [the mantra] of Ḍākinī;
oṃ lāme huṃ hūṃ phaṭ, [the mantra] of Lāmā.
Oṃ khaṇḍarohe huṃ hūṃ phaṭ; this is the mantra of Khaṇḍarohā, effective for all rites.
Oṃ rūpiṇīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
[This is] for Rūpiṇī.
Now, the mantras of Pracaṇḍā and the others are as follows: Oṃ pracaṇḍe huṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ caṇḍākṣīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ prabhāvatīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ mahānāse huṃ hūṃ phaṭ /
Oṃ vīramatīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ kharvarīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ laṅkeśvarīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ /
Oṃ drumacchāye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ airāvatīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ mahābhairavīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ /
Oṃ vāyuvege huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ surābhakṣīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ śyāmādevīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ /
Oṃ subhadre huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ hayakarṇe huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ khagānane huṃ hūṃ phaṭ /
Oṃ cakravege huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ khaṇḍarohe huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ śoṇḍinīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ /
Oṃ cakravarmaṇīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ mahāvīrye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ kākāsye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ /
Oṃ ulūkāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ śvānāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ śūkarāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ yamaḍādīye (yamaḍāḍhīye) hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ yamadūtīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ / Oṃ yamadaṃṣṭriṇīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ /
Oṃ yamamathanīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Thus, according to the *Abhisamayakrama* of Lūyīpāda,

the mandala-circle of the Blessed Goddess consisting of thirty-seven deities in its extensive form is now written down, as it was demonstrated by our gurus in the *Vajrāvalī* following the sequence of the various mandalas therein.
All the principal goddesses (nāyikā) and so forth have two arms, while the four ḍākinīs have four arms.
Kākāsyā and the others hold a skull-cup in their left hands and a khaṭvāṅga staff resting against their shoulders; in their right hands, they hold a hand-drum (ḍamaruka).
All other details are as previously described.
Alternatively, the Blessed Lady may be yellow or blue in color, while the four [consorts], Ḍākinī and the others, are yellow.
They hold a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) in their right hands.
The yoginīs of the *cītacakra* are white, with their left hands holding a vajra and making the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*).

Those of the speech wheel (*vākcakra*) are black, with their left hands holding a lotus and a threatening gesture (*tarjanīka*). Those of the body wheel (*kāyacakra*) are red, holding a threatening gesture and a wheel in their right hands.
Kākāsyā and the others hold a curved knife with the threatening forefinger in their right hands;
all the goddesses hold a skull-cup in their left hands.
Yamadāḍhī and the others hold a hand-drum in their right hands and a human skull with the threatening forefinger in their left hands.
In the left arms of the Ḍākinīs and others, as well as the Kākāsyās and others, there is a khaṭvāṅga.
These twelve dance in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka).
All else is as before.

For the sake of abandoning the ego-conception of a deity, for the attainment of omniscience, and for [the correct] vision, the Ḍākinīs and others should be understood as having the nature of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣikadharma*).

Among these, the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna*), characterized by the commencement of the full comprehension of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), is Ḍākinī. The application of mindfulness to feeling (*vedanānusmṛtyupasthāna*), characterized by the commencement of the full comprehension of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*), is Lāmā.
Because the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has the nature of an illusion, Khaṇḍarohā is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmānusmṛtyupasthāna*) characterized by retention.

Because of the purity of the specific distinctions in the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), Rūpiṇī is the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittānusmṛtyupasthāna*).
Pracaṇḍā is the basis of psychic power through zeal (*chanda-ṛddhipāda*), characterized by extreme devotion and the longing to hear the Dharma.
The base of psychic power of energy (*vīrya-ṛddhipāda*) is Caṇḍākṣī, characterized by the uninterrupted practice of vigor;
the base of psychic power of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-ṛddhipāda*) is Prabhāvatī, characterized by ultimate discernment;
and the base of psychic power of mind (*citta-ṛddhipāda*) is Mahānāsā, characterized by the excellence of the intention to realize awakening.
The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*)—which consists of conviction in the truths, the Three Jewels, karma and its results, as well as the mastery of determining reality—is Vīramatī.
The faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*)—which is the determination that [the practice] must necessarily be performed—is Kharvarī.
The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)—which is the antidote to ignorance, characterized by unimpaired memory and sovereign power—is Laṅkeśvarī.
The faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) is the "Tree-Shade" (*drumacchāyā*) because of its mastery over the excellence of the mind.
The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is "Airāvatī" because of its mastery in discerning what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.
These very faculties, beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), become "powers" (*bala*) when they reach the ultimate limit of their development.
The power of faith belongs to Mahābhiravā; the power of vigor belongs to Vāyuvegā;
the power of mindfulness belongs to Surābhakṣī.
The power of concentration is Śyāmādevī;
the power of wisdom is Subhadrā.
Concentration alone is the cause of awakening;
Hayakarṇā is the factor of awakening that is concentration. Khagānanā is the factor of awakening that is vigor, in which there is no room for indolence.
Zeal for wholesome qualities is the factor of awakening of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*), Cakravegā;
adaptability in wholesome action is the factor of awakening of tranquility (*prasrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), Khaṇḍarohā;
and ascertainment by way of the nature of selflessness is the factor of awakening of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), Śauṇḍinī.
The nature of non-forgetfulness is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, Cakravarmiṇī;
non-attention toward meditative concentration is the equanimity factor of enlightenment, Suvīrā;
and the practice of the non-perverted meaning is right view, Mahābalā.
The non-abandonment of what has been undertaken with earnest devotion is Right Resolve, who is Cakravartinī;
speech that does not deceive sentient beings is Right Speech, who is Mahāvīryā;
and action that does not transgress the ten wholesome paths is Right Action, who is Kākāsyā.
Livelihood that does not harm sentient beings is right livelihood, Ulūkāsyā; the accomplishment of wholesome goals is right effort, Śvānāsyā;
and the recollection of the Buddha’s words is right mindfulness, Śūkarāsyā.
Perfect concentration is the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī;
the production of unarisen wholesome qualities is Yamaḍāḍhī (Yamaḍāḍhī); and the preservation of arisen wholesome qualities is Yamadūtī.
The abandonment of unwholesome states that have already arisen is Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī; and the correct abandonment through the non-arising of unwholesome states that have not yet arisen is Yamamathanī.

Through the purification of the ten stages known as Pramuditā, Vimalā, Prabhākarī, Arciṣmatī, Abhimukhī, Sudurjayā, Dūraṅgamā, Acalā, Sādhumatī, and Dharmameghā, the internal yogin should sequentially meditate upon the body-maṇḍala in the form of the *pīṭhas*, *upapīṭhas*, and so forth.
Thus it is said in two verses of chapter 65 of the *Abhidhānottara*:
"The sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth are established here through twenty-four divisions."
Therefore, those who perceive reality should certainly not feel weary of that wandering.
"The afflictions of those external yogins are destroyed through wandering;
therefore, having rejected the external, one should abide in the system of the Yoginīs. Thus it is said.
There, at the crown of Pullīramalaya, is Pracaṇḍā: Oṃ Aṃ Goṃ Rāṃ Deṃ Māṃ Māṃ Oṃ Triṃ Kauṃ Kaṃ Laṃ Kāṃ Hiṃ Preṃ Gṛṃ Sauṃ Suṃ Naṃ Siṃ Maṃ Kuṃ.
Caṇḍākṣī is at Jalāndharaśikhā;
Prabhāvatī is at Oḍiyāna on the right ear;
Mahānāsā is at Arbuda on the back of the head.
The sacred seat (pīṭha):
Vīramatī is at the left ear of the Godāvarī;
Kharvarī is between the eyebrows at Rāmeśvara.
Lankeśvarī is at the two eyes of Devīkoṭa; Drmacchāyā is on the two shoulders of Mālava; these are the Upapīṭhas.
Khecarī belongs to the mind-wheel (cittacakra);
by her, those who have gone to heaven are gathered.
Airavatī [belongs] to the destruction of desire and form.
Mahābhairavā is in the pair of breasts in Oḍra;
Vāyuvegā is at the navel in Triśakuni.
Surābhakṣī is at the tip of the nose of Kauśāla; Śyāmādevī is at the mouth of Kaliṅga, which is a secondary field (upakṣetra).
Subhadrā is at Lampāka-kaṇṭha; it is a chandoha. Hayakarṇā is at Kāñcī-hṛdaya.
In the vulva of the Himalaya is Khagānanā;
this is Upacchandoha.
In the wheel of speech (vākcakra) is Bhūcarī.
By means of this, there is the gathering of mortals;
at the Pretapurī-liṅga is Cakravegā;
and at Gṛhadevatā-guḍa (or -guda) is Khaṇḍarohā.
Melāpaka:
Śauṇḍinī is at Saurāṣṭra on the two thighs;
Cakravarmiṇī is at Suvarṇadvīpa on the shanks.
Suvīrā is at the junction of the city-fingers; Mahābalā is at the back of the foot of the Sindhu.
In the cremation ground,
Cakravartinī is at the two big toes;
in Kulatā, Mahāvīryā is at the two knees.
Upaśmaśāna;
Kāyacare, who dwells in Pātāla.
By her, those who have gone to Pātāla are gathered.
In this regard, the instruction is as follows:
let all [the syllables] beginning with *puṃ*, *jāṃ*, and so forth, together with their *anusvāras*, be examined.

The locations such as the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*), which consist of the nature of the wheel of emptiness (*araśūnyatācakra*) pervaded by the syllables beginning with *puṃ* and the rest, are to be visualized instantaneously in the head and other parts of the body.
In those *pīṭhas* and other locations, the channels (*nāḍīs*) situated in their respective places should be visualized as being transformed into the forms of the corresponding deities;
just as rivers flowing near external trees and such are nourished by water.
Just as [the earth] performs [this function], so too do the channels (*nāḍī*) within the body nourish the nails and other parts; such is the similarity.
Externally, the site known as Mahābodhi is the Vajrapīṭha, and the river Nairañjanā is the channel (*nāḍī*);
internally, the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) is the Vajrapīṭha, and the *avadhūtī* is the Nirañjanā.
Kākāsyā and the others are the gatekeepers at the mouth, the left and right nostrils, and the anus in sequence;
Yamadāḍhī and the others are at the left and right ears and the left and right eyes;
and the four beginning with Ḍākinī are at the heart, forehead, throat, and navel lotuses.
Thus, one should repeatedly and firmly resolve upon the entire body-maṇḍala;
thereafter, one should offer the bali.

Having placed the food and other offerings before him and purified them according to the previously described sequence, he should visualize the mandala—the wheel perfected in all its aspects—brought forth by the *jālāmudrā* and its corresponding measure, and establish it before him. Having worshipped it with the *argha* and other offerings, he should behold the syllable *HŪṂ* situated between his two hands, which have the nature of the moon and sun mandalas produced from the vowels (*ali*) and consonants (*kāli*). Then he recites: *Oṃ, all phenomena are mutually interpenetrated; spread forth, spread forth! All phenomena have entered [into one another], they have utterly entered.*

Having first uttered "HŪṂ" for all phenomena, and having meditated upon that vessel of nectar placed within the palms joined in the vajra-añjali gesture through the transformation of the syllable HŪṂ mounted upon the moon and sun, one should recite this for the sake of attaining the desired siddhi:
"The goddesses are the authority, the samaya is the authority, and their spoken words are the supreme authority.
By this truth, may these goddesses become the cause of my grace."

Then, perceiving the non-duality of the object of worship, the worshiper, and the act of worship, one should rotate that vessel of nectar counter-clockwise through the cardinal directions starting from the east, and clockwise through the intermediate directions starting from the southeast. While rotating it, one should recite once the respective mantras of the deities of the three wheels for the principal consort—whose tongue is a white vajra born from the syllable *HŪṂ*—and [recite]:
*OṂ ARALLI HOḤ JAḤ HŪṂ VAṂ HOḤ VAJRAḌĀKINYAḤ SAMAYAS TVAM*.
With the mantra *dṛśyo ho*, uttered one, two, three, four, or five times,

he should offer [the deity]. Then, having given water for sipping (*ācamana*), water for sprinkling the hands (*hastaprokṣaṇa*), betel, and so forth, and having worshipped with lutes and other instruments and offered praise, he should make his petition.
Equanimous toward existence and peace, having shattered the very structure of conceptual constructs,
they perceive all phenomena as being like space; with the lord of their hearts swollen by the waters of profound compassion, they look upon reality from the perspective of its true nature.
O goddesses, show me your great compassion! Act! Cut [the bonds]! Act! Show me your great compassion!
Then, while rotating [the vessel] as before for the guardians of the directions stationed in the eight cremation grounds, one should offer by reciting twice:

"Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi! May all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, apasmāras, ḍākas, ḍākinīs, and so forth, accept this bali! Protect the samaya! Grant me all accomplishments! Eat, drink, smell, and enjoy as you wish! For the sake of increasing my true happiness in every way, be my helpers! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
Thus, by reciting this twice, one should perform the *ḍhakkana* offering.
From consuming that nectar, the guardians of the directions and the other deities should be visualized with their bodies endowed with great bliss.

Following that, having offered betel and other items collectively, one should worship them with lutes and other instruments emanating from the seed-syllable in one's own heart, praise them with the eight-line mantra, and pray for the attainment of the desired siddhi. Then, having stirred [the assembly] with the *cchoma* hand-gesture, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra preceded by the ringing of the bell in order to fulfill any deficiencies in the ritual procedure.
Thereafter—

Reciting "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga," and having satisfied [the deity] with the *kamalāvarta* mudrā, one should withdraw the mudrā and, preceded by the gesture of embracing, snap the left ring finger and thumb while reciting "Oṃ vajra mur."
Reciting thus, one should dismiss [the deities] and cause the maṇḍala to enter into oneself in its entirety. Then,
having made the aspiration prayer, one should dwell in the form of the deity.

At the time of bathing, one should perform the rite of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). At the time of eating, however, one should instantly visualize one’s own body as the nature of the maṇḍala-circle; having offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) according to the ritual rules and empowered that oblation with the three-syllable mantra, one should offer it to the guardians of the directions by reciting once the mantra beginning with *oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhī*, and so forth. Having purified [the food] through the procedure of kindling and so on, one should consume the eatables and other items according to the rule, with the pride of the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanatāsamatā*), having fashioned the tongue out of white vajra produced from the syllable *hūṃ*.
Having empowered [the water] with "Oṃ amṛtodaka hūṃ hūṃ ṭha ṭha trāṃ āḥ khaṃ hūṃ," one should satisfy the syllable *vaṃ* located at the navel by means of the three-syllable [mantra].
At the midday twilight, however, one should enter the house for meditation.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra body, speech, and mind of all yoginīs.
Oṃ, all phenomena are vajra-pure; I am vajra-pure.
Reciting these three mantras, one should instantly resolve upon the maṇḍala circle, perform everything as before, and dwell at ease.

At the twilight of midnight, having performed everything as at the midday twilight, and having realized that all vocal activity consists of the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*), one should recite from *a* to *kṣa*, followed by *huṃ hūṃ phaṭ paṭ*. Having brought the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*) face-to-face, one should go to sleep while resolving upon the state of Clear Light even during sleep.
At the conclusion of all twilights, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra.
Furthermore, at the dawn twilight, having resolved upon the maṇḍala circle arisen from luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), one should perform all that was previously described.
Thus, the procedure for external worship is stated:

here, a mantra practitioner desiring to worship the Blessed Lady, having risen in the morning or at an appropriate time, and being endowed with the yoga of Vajravairocanī, should place his hand upon a clean spot.

Having recited the mantra beginning with *oṃ sumbha ni-sumbha*, one should smear a square maṇḍala with a pill made of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), fragrant substances, and so forth, or with a pill of cow dung mixed with any one of those substances. Having drawn a cross in the center of that, one should recite the twenty-four syllables of the *pūjā* mantra and the ten names beginning with *pīṭha* and *upapīṭha*, preceded by the mental visualization (*adhimokṣa*) of each respective location.

Then, having visualized within that mandala the syllable *Sūṃ* upon a sun disk resting on a red lotus atop Mount Sumeru—which stands upon the four great elements—one should see the Wisdom Mandala brought there by its rays and enter therein; one should then behold the Blessed Lady together with her retinue, fully perfected in all aspects, as the transformation of that [syllable].

Then, having performed worship with the goddesses such as Vīṇā who have emerged from the seed-syllable at one's own heart, and having offered the seven jewels and so forth emerging from that [mandala], one should offer a flower to the Blessed Lady in the center of the mandala with the three syllables, using the left hand purified according to the ritual rule.
Furthermore, one should offer [the oblation] there with the *hṛdaya* and *upahṛdaya* mantras of the Bhagavatī.

Then, flowers should be placed upon the mandala in their respective positions: for the deities beginning with Ḍākinī and ending with Yamamathanī, using their individual mantras, in a counter-clockwise direction in the cardinal directions and in a clockwise direction in the intermediate directions.

Subsequently, according to the sequence of hand-worship (*hastapūjā*) to be described, one should offer flowers with their respective mantras, such as *oṃ ha*, to the deities positioned on the hands in their corresponding locations.

Then, having cast the flower held in the left hand into the mandala while reciting the eight-syllable mantra, and having placed his joined palms to his head, he should cause the wheel of deities held in the palm of his hand to enter into himself.

Following that, having praised with the heart-mantra and other eight-syllable mantras as well as the hymns of praise as they were performed, and having performed the confession of sins and so forth, as well as meditation, mantra-recitation, and the making of aspirations according to his ability, he should utter the hundred-syllable mantra:
*oṃ yogaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmā yogaśuddho ’ham*.

Having thus satisfied [the deity] with the *kamalāvarta* mudrā accompanied by the mantra, and while performing the gesture of embracing preceded by the withdrawal of the mudrā together with the snapping of the fingers, one should dismiss [the deity] while reciting "Oṃ vajra mur," and cause that maṇḍala-circle to enter into oneself.
Then, it should be understood that one should erase the lines in the maṇḍala.
Now, the procedure for the hand-worship (*hastapūjā*) is described.

There, in the circle of qualities (*guṇamaṇḍala*) and so forth, the yogi who possesses the yoga of Śrī Vajravārāhī should place the syllable *haṃ*—representing the natures of Vajrasattva, Vairocana, Amitābha, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, and Amoghasiddhi—in the tips of the fingers of his left hand, namely the thumb, index finger, middle finger, ring finger, and little finger, which are respectively white, yellow, red, black, and green in color, while reciting the mantras: *oṃ*, *namaḥ*, *hi*, *svāhā*, *hu*, *vauṣaṭ*, *he*, *huṃ*, *hūṃ*, *hoḥ*, *phaṭ*.

Having meditated on a five-petalled lotus, reddish in color, instantly manifested upon the palm of the hand, one should visualize the seed-syllables *haṃ yoṃ hriṃ moṃ hreṃ hriṃ huṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ* in due order, moving counter-clockwise from the eastern petal through the petals of the directions, which correspond respectively to the forms of Yāminī, Mohinī, Sañcāraṇī, Saṃtrāsanī, and Caṇḍikā, and possess the colors blue, white, yellow, green, smoky, and greyish-white.

In the center of the [lotus] disc, one should clearly visualize the seed-syllable *oṃ vaṃ*, red in color and having the nature of Vajravārāhī, or its reflection as the three wheels (*tricakra*), even upon the back of the hand.
Then, one should resolve that the elements of earth, water, fire, air, and space contained within the hands have the nature of Pātanī, Māraṇī, Ākarṣaṇī, Narteśvarī, and Padmajālinī.

Next, having smeared the seed-syllables residing in those hands with the liquid substance, one should resolve that the palm of the hand has the form of the three wheels presided over by all the yoginīs.

One should offer liquid substances and so forth with either a three-syllable mantra or an eight-word mantra. Then, having performed worship, one should recite the *Śatākṣara* [mantra] for the purpose of fulfilling any deficiencies or excesses in the ritual procedure. Having requested the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the wheel and other [deities], one should place that liquid in another vessel or elsewhere. Then, using the substance held in the hand—grasped by the left ring finger—one should anoint the heart, tongue, and head while uttering the syllables *HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ*. One should then resolve that the host of deities has entered into oneself.
This ritual procedure is well-known from the *Saṃcāra-tantra*.

Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the worship of the hands (*hastapūjāvidhi*). Alternatively, while reciting the ten names of the *pīṭhas*, *upapīṭhas*, and so forth, with the ring finger of the left hand purified by the previously mentioned rite, one should draw two intersecting triangles (*puṭa*) using liquor purified according to the rules. In their center, one should draw a circular mandala. Therein, having visualized the Blessed Lady—emerging from the seed-syllable of one’s own heart, drawn forth by that very instrument, and accompanied by the circle of the support and the supported—one should offer her food, drink, and so forth, prepared in the form of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and other substances, using either the three-syllable mantra or the eight-line mantra.

Having taken the *madana* (intoxicant), which has become like nectar (*amṛta*) placed in a lotus vessel, with the thumb and ring finger, one should satisfy the Blessed Lady with her heart-mantra and near-heart-mantra, and likewise satisfy those beginning with Ḍākinī and ending with Yamamathanī with their respective mantras.

Then, having performed worship and recited the hundred-syllable mantra for the purpose of fulfilling any deficiencies or excesses in the ritual procedure, and having made the request for the consecration of the *gaṇacakra*, [one should say]:
*oṃ yogaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmā yogaśuddho ’ham*.

Reciting thus, one should satisfy [the deities] with the *kamalāvarta* mudrā; then, withdrawing that mudrā while performing a gesture of embracing and touching the ground with the ring finger, one should dismiss them by reciting *oṃ vajra mur* and cause that maṇḍala to enter into oneself. Then, taking the *madana* (intoxicant) that has fallen upon the ground with the left ring finger, one should smear it upon the heart, tongue, and head while uttering the syllables *hūṃ āḥ oṃ*. One should then visualize that the circle of deities residing in that [substance] has also entered into oneself. This is called "worship with the hand."

Then, with *oṃ śukla*, one should offer the other oblations (*itarāhuti*) with the right *sruva* ladle—[the tongue] transformed into a vajra—into the mandalas filled with garlands of flames situated upon the pericarp of the lotus of one’s own navel.
This is the remainder of the internal fire offering (*adhyātmahoma*).
*Oṃ āḥ ucchiṣṭavajra adhitiṣṭhemaṃ baliṃ hūṃ svāhā.*

In the fire of the gnosis that has the form of the wheel of the three realms—non-dual in its emptiness and compassion—the supreme *homa* consists of burning the fuel of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, according to the oral instructions.

As for external *homa*s such as those for pacification (*śāntika*) and enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), they should be performed following the *homa* ritual manual, in accordance with the specific rites, by attending to the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), flowers, fuel-sticks (*samidh*), drying, and other requirements.
The detailed procedures have not been written here for fear of prolixity.
Thus, the visualization of the mandala of the Bhagavatī has been explained in detail, including the procedures for offerings, bali-oblations, and so forth.

However, for one who prefers a medium [scale] practice, one should visualize a fivefold mandala consisting of the four—Ḍākinī and the others—in the cardinal petals, the substances of the pledge (*samayadravya*) placed in lotus vessels in the intermediate petals, and the Bhagavatī as described above in the center.
As for the bali-offerings, worship, and other rites, they should be performed for these five with their respective mantras as appropriate.
The protection wheel and so forth are exactly as before.
Furthermore, according to the sequence emerging from Oḍiyāna, she stands with her feet upward;
the seed-syllable for her accomplishment and the mantras beginning with the heart-mantra are those very same ones.
The ḍākinīs and others are likewise.
However, one who seeks a concise practice meditates solely on the Blessed Lady in the form already described.
The worship and other rites should be performed for the Blessed Lady as previously stated.

In some cases, having worshipped the Buddhas and others brought forth by the rays of the white syllable *oṃ* situated upon the moon of one’s own heart, and having meditated upon emptiness, she is visualized as the Moon-Vajra (*candravajra*), produced from the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, seated upon a lotus and moon.
Furthermore, this very Blessed Lady is called Vajravairocanī and Vajrayoginī.
And regarding her, there are many varieties of oral traditions (*āmnāya*) according to the scriptures and the instructions.

For example, one should visualize oneself as the Blessed Lady Kolāsyā, who has many bellies, with reddish-brown hair on her head, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture upon a corpse, and red in color. Above a triangular fire-mandala arising from the syllable *raṃ* located at one's own navel, one sees a red circular lotus and a red syllable *hrīṃ*. Through the complete transformation of all that, she holds in her two right hands a vajra and a goad, and in her two left hands a *khaṭvāṅga*, a skull-cup, and a noose with a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*).
Her remaining form is as described previously; this is the procedure of the venerable Vajraghoṇā.
The specific difference, however, is the heart mantra: *oṃ hūṃ hrīṃ traṃ*.
Oṃ vajravārāhi āveśaya sarvaduṣṭān hrīṃ svāhā—this is the *upahṛdaya* (near-heart mantra).
This characteristic is accomplished through recitation preceded by the yoga of the Goddess; of this there is no doubt.
With this mantra, one should offer incense made from powdered *mahāmāṃsa*.
In twenty-one days before the cloth [painting], the desired goal is accomplished.
One should utter the syllables: *oṃ hrīṃ haṃ hāṃ haḥ haḥ hiḥ hīṃḥ hīṃḥ hīṃḥ i pheṃ pheṃ*.
For the purpose of pacifying all Māras, an offering of food at night should be presented with the fivefold service (*pañcopacāra*).
This procedure is not to be revealed to those who are unworthy;
by this, the Vajrayoginīs bestow their blessing. Oṃ hrīṃ ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Having first offered the *bali* with this [mantra], one should perform this *sādhana* of Vajraghoṇā.
Although the ritual procedure for the *bali* and so forth has already been mentioned previously, it is performed here as well;
for what is additional is indeed more praiseworthy.

In some cases, she arises from the transformation of a red five-pronged vajra, which is presided over by the syllable *hrīṃ*—white (or pale-white)—situated upon a sun disc born from the syllable *āṃ* within a heart-lotus of blood. She stands in the *ālīḍha* posture atop a sleeping man of ignorance (the *ajñānapuruṣa*) who rests upon a sun disc on a white (or pale-white) and red lotus. Her heart is a vajra situated on a sun disc presided over by a red *hrīṃ* situated on a sun disc. She receives consecration from Akṣobhya, who is situated on a sun disc atop a double lotus (*viśvapadma*). All else is as before.

Thereafter, having visualized the syllable *Hrīḥ* within a red and white solar disc situated upon a universal lotus at one's navel, one should imagine it as a white rosary of its mantra-beads. By means of the "wheel-rotation" yoga, one should draw it out through the opening of the mouth, taking with it the power of the multitude of Buddha-qualities, mantras, medicinal gems, the moon and stars, scripts, treatises, arts, and so forth. One should meditate on it entering the opening of the navel, consisting of the burning away of all ignorance in oneself and others.
One should recite the mantra—free from defects such as rapidity or slowness—as follows:
*Hrīṃ Hrīṃ*.
When one wishes to rise, then, having internalized the mantra-garland within the syllable *hrīṃ* at the navel and performed the worship and other rites, one should dwell as one pleases.

Furthermore, having visualized upon one's own tongue—which has the appearance of a lotus petal born from the syllable *āḥ*—the red syllable *hrīṃ* in a blazing and radiant form, and having stabilized the mind there, one should recite [the mantra] with a rosary of fifty beads during the four or three junctions of the day.

Thus, a yogi endowed with the practice of recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*bhāvanā*), through seven hundred thousand recitations, becomes one who is proficient in all scriptures and arts, intelligent, a good retainer of knowledge, invincible in assemblies, a debater, and a great poet. He cannot be withered or afflicted by fevers, spiders, *ḍākinīs*, and the like. When this mantra has been perfected, if a pen consecrated with the proper measure of it is placed in anyone's hand, even that person, though a fool, becomes a poet.

To subjugate her, one should visualize her as red in color and, having performed the tasting of nectar according to the ritual rules, see the person to be accomplished—produced from the syllables of one's own name—as being drawn in by rays of light emerging from the mantra-garland and brought before oneself. Then, observing that [person] has the form of a red moon disc transformed from the *cittamoḥ* syllable, one should visualize the goddess emerging from that mantra-garland, red in color, holding a noose marked with the syllable *hrīḥ* in her left hand and a vajra-hook resembling the bud of a red lotus in her right, standing before the person to be accomplished.

Then, following the command "Oṃ āḥ hrīḥ, attract the mind of [Name]! Hūṃ jaḥ!", that goddess enters the body of the subject according to the ritual procedure; she encircles the moon-maṇḍala of his mind with her noose and, prodding it with her hook, draws it into her own mind and merges into the mantra-garland.
Then, one should meditate upon that subject with palms joined, solitary, completely under control, facing the practitioner, and saying, "What shall I do?
One should meditate in this way at the four junctions of the day or at three; before long, one will certainly bring the subject under control.

In another [form], however, she stands upon a moon disc on a universal lotus, arisen from the transformation of a red *hūṃ* syllable. She tramples corpses with her legs in the *ālīḍha* and *pratyālīḍha* postures; her hair is red and blazing upward. She has two arms: the right hand brandishes a severed [skull-topped staff] with the index finger extended, and the left holds a skull-cup filled with blood. All other ornaments and attributes are as before. *Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye oṃ vajravarṇanīye oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.* This is the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Oṃ vajraḍākinīye hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā / This is the heart mantra. Oṃ vajrayoginīye hūṃ phaṭ svāhā /
The subsidiary heart-mantra (*upahṛdayamantra*):
*oṃ vajraḍākinīye imaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa ha ha ha ha kha kha kha kha a a a a mama siddhiṃ prayaccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having consecrated the offering (*bali*) with this mantra as before by means of the nectar-rite (*amṛtīkṛtya*), it should be presented.
Specifically, on the eighth day and so forth, it should be offered at night in a cremation ground.
In some places, she is seen born from a red *hūṃ* syllable, with a crown and a mass of curly hair; in other places, she is without a corpse.
The mantras, however, are those same ones.

In some [traditions], she herself arises from a yellow syllable *hrīḥ* in the center of the Dharmodaya, which is vermilion-red and situated upon a sun disk atop a white lotus in her own navel; she holds with her left hand a severed head, while her right hand wields a flaying knife. Her left arm is extended upward, her right arm is bent downward, her right leg is stretched out, and her left foot is drawn in.

A stream of blood, having issued from the *kabandha* through the path of the *avadhūtī*, falls into her mouth; others, having issued from the *lalanā* and *rasanā*, enter the mouths of the two deities on the sides. Thus it should be visualized: on the left side is Śyāmavarṇā Vajravarṇanī, holding a curved knife (*kartī*) in her left hand and a skull-cup (*kapāla*) in her right, with her left leg extended and her right leg contracted.
On the right side is Pītavarṇā Vajravairocanī, holding a curved knife in her right hand and a skull-cup in her left, with her right foot extended and her left foot contracted.
The rest is as before.
Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye, oṃ vajravarṇanīye, oṃ vajravairocanīye, hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. This is the mantra for recitation.
Regarding worship:
having drawn the *dharmodayā* above the sun situated within a square maṇḍala, and having meditated upon the syllable *hrīṃ* in its center, one should perform worship.
One should worship the Blessed Lady born from that [syllable], who possesses the form described above.
Therein, in the center of the *dharmodayā*,
one should first worship with the mantra beginning: *oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye*.
With the mantra "oṃ sarvaḍākinīye hūṃ svāhā," one should offer the water for honor (*argha*) and so forth;
[this is done] on the left.
Oṃ vajravarṇanīye hūṃ svāhā.
To the right: Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ svāhā.
Thus one should worship.

Then, having worshipped each of the Oḍḍiyāna, Pūrṇagiri, Kāmarūpa, Śrīhaṭṭa, Dharma, Saṃbhoga, Nirmāṇa, and Mahāsukha bodies by interweaving their names ending in the dative case with the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and *svāhā* at the end, one should dismiss them as before.
However, in another ritual procedure, one should resolve that one’s own body is the celestial palace (*kūṭāgāra*) purified of the three realms.

Instantly, in the navel-center, one should visualize the goddess Bhavānī, who has the color of a hibiscus flower, sits in the half-lotus posture, performs the *tāṇḍava* dance, and holds a curved knife and a skull-cup in her hands.
Her right face is that of a boar, and her left is a wrathful face;
these two faces are said to represent the purification of the two truths. Thus it is stated.

Thus, having taken this up, one should understand that there are infinite traditions of the Blessed Lady descending through the lineage of the instructions of the Siddhas, due to the differences in the dispositions of those to be trained (*vineyāśaya*).
This has been shown merely as a direction.

And among these sequences, by adopting a single sequence, one who possesses faith and so forth, who is free from attachment, who observes the commitments (*samaya*), and who meditates without doubt, will certainly achieve success.
The preliminary worship as it has come down in the oral instructions is written here:

On the tenth day, having wiped [the surface] with saffron and other substances, one should drop vermilion into a stainless vessel; having drawn a *dharmodayā* in its center with a golden stylus, one should write the syllable *hrīṃ* in its center.
Then, having drawn the Nandyāvarta mudrā on the side, one should worship it with water and flowers.
One should first worship the four seats (pīṭhas), beginning with Oḍiyāna, as well as the four bodies.
One should offer whatever is available of the pledge-substances (samayadravya), such as food and drink.
And one should worship a maiden.

This ritual must be performed in strict secrecy by one who is naked with disheveled hair, seated facing south; otherwise, there will be a loss of accomplishment and various kinds of diseases will arise.

Then, having offered the bali-oblation and made a prayer for the desired success, and having dismissed [the deity], one should give the vermilion, the food offering, and so forth, to young maidens or to women whose husbands are living.

Furthermore, on the tenth, eighth, or fourteenth [lunar day], whatever flowers, fruits, oil, betel, rice, vegetables, leaves, curd, wood, salt, vermilion, fish, or meat may be sold by women such as Māmakī and others, one should purchase some small amount of whatever is available according to one's means. Having prepared it appropriately as before, one should write the seed-syllables and so forth within a *dharmodaya* fashioned from vermilion, worship it, pray for the attainment of one's desired goal, and then dismiss it.
From this point onwards, as before, it is taught that in dreams there will be consolation from the Vajra-women.

Furthermore, on the eighth day, having applied vermilion (*sindūra*) upon the surface of a perfectly polished mirror, one should draw the *dharmodaya-mudrā* therein; having written the seed-syllable *vaṃ* in the outer corners and the mantra in the center, and having drawn a *nandyāvarta* in a counter-clockwise direction on the four sides outside the *dharmodayā*, one should worship it with flowers and other offerings, recite the mantra as many times as possible, and place that "recitation-vermilion" together in a single vessel.
One should perform this for as long as six months.
Then, having placed that vermilion inside a *lāṅgalī* plant that is poisonous and blue in its center, one should bury it in a cremation ground.
Having performed the offering (*bali*) and worship, one should recite the mantra according to one's desire.
In this manner, one should perform this for one month every day.
Having fashioned a *tilaka* in the shape of a *nandyāvarta* with that vermilion (*sindūra*), one should enter the village for alms.
Whichever woman is seen upon whom that *tilaka* has been transferred, she should be won over with effort.
Thus, by means of the *nandyāvarta* [diagram], is the ritual for the propitiation of Vajrayoginī according to the tradition of the Siddha Śabarapāda.
Furthermore, in this system of the Yoginīs, one who abides in it should perform worship, mantra-recitation, eating, and so forth, secretly with the left hand.
For those performing a pilgrimage to sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and other sites, a circumambulation of villages, cities, and so forth should be performed counter-clockwise in honor of the Vajraḍākinīs.
When traveling, one should proceed by first extending the left foot forward.
Whatever the five objects of desire (*pañcakāma*) may be encountered, they should be enjoyed without hesitation, as the purification of Vairocana and the other [Buddhas].
One must not perform rites of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) against those who are well-behaved or innocent.

Women must not be beaten, nor should they be provoked to anger, nor should they be held in contempt; this applies especially to those who bear the six mudrās. Having understood these various types of commitments (*samaya*) according to the tantras, they should be observed. Mantras and other such elements should also be learned from that very source and employed accordingly.
They are not written here for fear of prolixity;
what need is there to say more?
The Buddha is the teacher, the Dharma is the teacher, and likewise, the Saṅgha is the teacher.
The glorious Guru is Vajradhara; the Guru alone is the cause here.
"Therefore, one who desires the fruit of Buddhahood should propitiate the Guru. Having thus established this,
if the virtuous desire to enjoy immediately the fruit of peace— this universe, made beautiful by the fragrance of the flowers of its qualities— [they should do so through the Guru].
Therefore, with effort, one should attain this new, overflowing cluster of blossoms arising from the wish-fulfilling tree of clear realization.
Having extracted a small portion from the tantras, the abhisamayas, the upāyas, the sādhanas, and even from the words of the guru, this work has been composed without confusion.
By this merit which I have acquired, arising from this emanation,
may the world through its practice attain the exalted state of the Vajra Consort.
The *Śrīvajrayoginīsādhana*, titled *Abhisamayamañjarī*, composed by the great master Śubhākaragupta, is completed.
